A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, renamed from PRISM to SISL. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and the methods, equations, tables and figures can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on Kitchen, Office, Maze2D and AntMaze, including benchmark returns, learning curves, ablations and skill visualizations.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds data-quality and data-size experiments, reward-model measurements, runtime measurements and component ablations.

M1.justification: PRISM's exploration policy and buffer are renamed as SISL's skill-improvement policy and buffer. The objectives, prioritization, periodic skill deployment, high-level policy reinitialization and meta-test procedure remain equivalent. The additional buffer-reset description in Appendix G.4 is newly disclosed detail, without evidence that the procedure changed.

E1.justification: The four environments and their task definitions remain unchanged. Within Kitchen, v3 adds random-action corruption and medium-quality or uniformly random demonstrations, extending the evaluated data conditions beyond expert and Gaussian-corrupted demonstrations (Appendices D.3-D.4).

E2.justification: Table 1 retains SAC, SAC+RND, PEARL, PEARL+RND, SPiRL and SiMPL. The new robustness comparisons reuse SPiRL and SiMPL; no external comparator is added or removed from a corresponding retained experiment. New component-removal variants are ablations.

E3.justification: v3 substantially extends the evaluation design with Kitchen dataset-size controls at 50%, 25% and 10%, random action replacement at 25%, 50% and 100%, and expert/medium/random comparisons. It also evaluates reward-model MSE and runtime. Existing task splits, training budgets, horizons and tabulated hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds robustness studies of data scarcity, unstructured corruption and demonstration quality, plus reward-model accuracy across noise levels and quantitative state-action coverage analysis. Appendix G.4 separately ablates RND and high-level policy reinitialization. The earlier buffer, prioritization-temperature and KL-coefficient ablations and skill visualizations are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five random seeds and standard deviations shown through shaded regions and table uncertainties. The additional results follow this reporting practice; no increased run count, confidence interval procedure or significance test is introduced.

E6.justification: All 64 mean/standard-deviation pairs in Table 1 are unchanged. Substantial new results appear in the appendices: SISL achieves 3.28±0.15 with 10% Kitchen expert data and 1.68±0.18 with random data. Removing reinitialization yields 0.41±0.11 versus full SISL's 3.48±0.07 at Gaussian noise σ=0.3. Reward-model errors, coverage percentages and runtime measurements are also newly reported.

T1.justification: Equations (1)-(7) and the appendix loss definitions remain mathematically equivalent after notation changes and reordering. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs that are added or removed. New stability and curriculum explanations are informal interpretations.

C1.justification: v3 explicitly claims to be the first framework addressing suboptimal demonstrations in skill-based meta-RL through both exploration-guided refinement and relabeling, and adds an accelerated-convergence claim in the introduction. The central contributions and claims of robust adaptation through skill refinement and maximum return relabeling remain.

C2.justification: v3 adds a reward-model stability argument, identifies potential bias from differing task reward scales and suggests per-task standardization (Section 5.4 and Appendix F.4). Its limitations replace v1's qualitative description of comparable per-iteration computation with a measured 16% overhead. The meta-test fine-tuning limitation is retained.

D1.justification: v3 adds baseline repository links, reports training runtime, documents resetting the high-level buffer during reinitialization and offers a temperature-selection guideline. Its reproducibility statement says anonymized SISL code accompanies supplementary material, although availability cannot be verified from the PDFs. Existing architecture, hardware and hyperparameter details are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds targeted references, including Kipf et al., Rana et al. and Schmidt et al., and explicitly distinguishes reward-free skill learning from offline-to-online RL. It also excludes Yu et al. (2024b) and Wu et al. from its skill-learning category. Reset-related citations are added in G.4, while several exploration/self-supervision references are removed.

P1.justification: Beyond renaming PRISM to SISL, v3 extensively rewrites the contribution and methodology narrative around decoupled policies and self-improvement. It reorganizes appendix analyses, retains pseudocode only in the appendix, condenses environment descriptions, moves limitations into the main text and adds reproducibility and LLM-use statements.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a two-column ICML layout to a single-column ICLR layout. Figures 2 and 3 are redrawn, environment and learning-curve panels are rearranged, and retained analyses and algorithms are relocated. Five result tables are added: D.1-D.3, F.1 and G.1.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the central robustness claim beyond v1's Gaussian-corruption experiments through scarce-data, random-corruption and medium/random-demonstration tests. New RND/reset ablations and runtime measurements address important validation and computational-cost gaps. One added explanation is inconsistent: F.4 says the reward-model buffers contain no offline data, whereas Section 4.2 initializes the prioritized buffer from offline data. Despite this weakness, the expanded controlled evidence provides a substantial net improvement.
